note: Reads the cipherSuiteLen field from the ClientHello message at offset 39 (38-byte ssl_tls_client_server_hello + 1-byte sessionIDLength + 0 sessionID). The attacker sets this to 0xFFFF, so the function returns 32767 cipher suites without verifying that the actual message data contains that many 2-byte cipher suite entries.

The fuzz target iterates i from 0 to getCipherSuiteCount()-1 (32766). For index values >= 1, the index passes this bounds check because getCipherSuiteCount() returns the inflated count of 32767 based solely on the length field.

code: size_t cipherSuiteStartOffset = sizeof(ssl_tls_client_server_hello) + sizeof(uint8_t) + getSessionIDLength() + sizeof(uint16_t);
note: Computes cipherSuiteStartOffset = 38 + 1 + 0 + 2 = 41. This is the offset where the first cipher suite entry begins in the message data.

The bounds check only verifies that at least one 2-byte cipher suite exists (offset 41 + 2 = 43 <= m_DataLen). The attacker crafts the message so m_DataLen is exactly 43, meaning only the first cipher suite entry (2 bytes at offsets 41-42) is within bounds. The check does NOT verify that cipherSuiteStartOffset + 2*(index+1) <= m_DataLen for the requested index.

For index=1, reads 2 bytes at offset 41 + 2*1 = 43, which is exactly one byte past the end of the 43-byte message buffer (valid offsets 0-42). This causes a heap-buffer-overflow READ 2 in ASAN. The read at offset 43 accesses memory beyond the allocated heap buffer for the SSL handshake message data.

code: for (int i = 0; i < clientHelloMessage->getCipherSuiteCount(); i++) { clientHelloMessage->getCipherSuite(i); bool valid; clientHelloMessage->getCipherSuiteID(i, valid); }
note: The fuzz target calls getCipherSuiteID(i, valid) for every i from 0 to 32766. When i=1, the vulnerable bounds check in getCipherSuiteID passes (since only the first 2-byte entry is checked), but the actual read at cipherSuiteStartPos+1 goes out of bounds, triggering the heap-buffer-overflow.
